passage:
Hi Sabina di,
Nothing much here. College is fine, food is fine, hostel is fine. Ma keeps asking if I'm eating, and I keep saying yes, which is true. My phone got cracked, but it's fine. I didn't get into the cricket team, but I shrugged and it was fine. The roommate snores, but that's fine too. Okay, I've just noticed how many times I've typed that word. It doesn't matter really. I just didn't want to make a fuss when you're busy with your own exams. Anyway, good luck for yours. Maybe call one Sunday, if you have time. I wouldn't mind hearing your voice.
Karthik

qa.q: Which team did Karthik not get into?
qa.a: Karthik didn't get into the cricket team.

qa.q: What might Karthik be feeling underneath all the 'fine'?
qa.a: Karthik may be disappointed about the team and a bit lonely, and plays it down so as not to make a fuss, though the request for a call hints at wanting contact.

qa.q: How could Sabina reply to keep the door open?
qa.a: Sabina could call on Sunday, ask easy questions about small things, and let Karthik know there is time to talk whenever Karthik wants.

qa.q: How might Sabina read Karthik's letter?
qa.a: Sabina might notice how often Karthik writes 'fine' and the wish for a Sunday call, and sense that Karthik is lonelier than the letter says.

grounding: A teen plays feelings down with 'fine' and a shrug to avoid drama, but leaves a small opening for a trusted person.

passage: Manjula, you asked how I usually react when something goes wrong. Honestly, I shrug. "It's fine," I say, even when it's not. When my drawing wasn't picked for the school exhibition, I shrugged, went upstairs and drew for two hours. I don't like people fussing over me. It feels like too much attention and I never know what to say. My grandmother noticed anyway. She never asked me straight. She just said, "The kitchen light stays on late, and there's always something warm on the stove." That night I went down. I ate a bit, and then said, "I really wanted that one." She only nodded. I'm Devika, and I'm still a shrugger, but I know where the kitchen light is.

qa.q: What did Devika do for two hours after the drawing wasn't picked?
qa.a: Devika went upstairs and drew for two hours.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when saying 'It's fine'?
qa.a: Devika was disappointed and wanted privacy, as the later words 'I really wanted that one' show.

qa.q: What did Devika's grandmother do that worked?
qa.a: She left the door open without pressing, saying the kitchen light stayed on late, so Devika could come when ready.

qa.q: How might Devika's grandmother have felt seeing Devika shrug?
qa.a: She probably worried a little but respected Devika's privacy, choosing to wait quietly instead of asking straight out.

grounding: A teen plays feelings down with a shrug and 'it's fine' to avoid drama, and a trusted adult leaves the door open.

passage:
I'm Hansa, and I watched my brother Madhav come home the day the district team list came out. His name wasn't on it. He'd been practising every morning for a year.
Mummy asked, "How did it go?" He shrugged. "Fine. Didn't get in. Whatever." Then he went to his room.
He wasn't slamming doors. He wasn't crying. He ate dinner. He watched TV. If you didn't know him, you'd think he didn't care.
I couldn't tell if he really didn't care or was hiding it. Madhav always plays things down. He hates drama.
Mummy didn't push. But before bed she knocked and said, "I know you said fine. If it stops being fine, I'm here. Tonight or next week."
Three days later, I heard them talking late in the kitchen. He was saying, "I really thought I'd make it."
The door she left open, he walked through when he was ready.

qa.q: How long had Madhav been practising?
qa.a: Every morning for a year.

qa.q: What might Madhav have been feeling behind his "Fine. Whatever"?
qa.a: Madhav was probably disappointed and hurt after a year of practice, but played it down to avoid drama.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped?
qa.a: She didn't push, but left the door open by saying she'd be there whenever fine stopped being fine.

qa.q: What would change if Mummy had insisted he talk that night?
qa.a: Madhav might have closed up more, since he hates drama and needed time before he was ready.

grounding: A sister's account shows a teenager understating his disappointment with a shrug and "fine," and a parent leaving the door open.

passage:
Monday: A group of boys in Kamal's class had started calling him names in the corridor. When Mr Nilesh, the class teacher, asked if everything was okay, Kamal shrugged. "Fine, Sir. Nothing."
Mr Nilesh noticed he'd moved to the last bench and stopped raising his hand.
Wednesday: Mr Nilesh stopped Kamal after class. He didn't ask about the boys. He said, "You don't have to tell me anything. But if something's bothering you, I'm in the staff room every day at lunch. My door's open."
Kamal said, "Okay, Sir," and left quickly.
Friday: At lunch, Kamal stood in the staff room doorway for a while before knocking. "Sir... it's not nothing." He told him about the names.
Mr Nilesh listened, thanked him, and spoke to the boys and their class that afternoon. Kamal moved back to his old bench the next week.

qa.q: Where did Kamal move in class?
qa.a: To the last bench.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling behind "Fine, Sir. Nothing"?
qa.a: Kamal was hurt and probably embarrassed by the name-calling, but played it down to avoid drama or looking weak.

qa.q: Why did Mr Nilesh's approach work?
qa.a: He noticed the quiet changes, didn't force Kamal to talk, and offered a clear open door, which Kamal used when ready.

qa.q: How did Mr Nilesh read the shrug and "fine"?
qa.a: He didn't take it at face value; he noticed Kamal's withdrawal and suspected a real need behind the understatement.

grounding: The three beats show a teenager understating trouble with "fine," and a trusted adult leaving the door open until he is ready.

passage:
Shalini, you always say "it's nothing" when something's heavy. Let your Yamini Nani tell you about when she did the same.
When I was fifteen, my father fell ill and was in hospital for two months. At school, when friends asked, I shrugged. "It's nothing. He's fine." I didn't want pity. I didn't want to cry in class. So I made it small.
But at home I wasn't sleeping. I'd stopped eating lunch.
My aunt, Kamla Masi, noticed. She never forced me to talk. But every evening she'd sit on the verandah with her knitting and say, "I'm here, if it stops being nothing."
For three weeks I walked past her. Then one night I sat down, and I cried until the knitting was wet.
That open door, Shalini, was the most important thing anyone did for me that year. So when you're ready, I'm here.

qa.q: How long was Yamini's father in hospital?
qa.a: For two months.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling behind her "It's nothing"?
qa.a: She was frightened and deeply worried about her father, but hid it to avoid pity and crying in class.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Yamini Nani's story?
qa.a: Kamla Masi leaving the door open every evening without forcing her, until Yamini finally sat down and cried.

qa.q: How might Yamini's school friends have read her shrug?
qa.a: They probably believed it really was nothing, since she made it look small.

grounding: The elder's story shows a teenager understating a heavy worry with "it's nothing," and a trusted adult leaving the door open.

passage: The auto was stuck in the flooded underpass for forty minutes, rain drumming on the canvas roof, and Mohit had said exactly one word since his father, Shankar, picked him up from cricket camp. "Fine." "Selection list came out today, na?" Shankar tried. Mohit shrugged. "Yeah. Not in. Whatever. It's fine." He stared at a scooter half floating in the brown water outside. Shankar noticed the kit bag still zipped, the gloves Mohit always hung off it tucked away inside. He wanted to ask twenty questions. But the driver was listening, the horns were deafening, and Mohit's jaw was set. So Shankar only said, "Okay. If it stops being fine, or even if it stays fine, I'm up late tonight. Chai at eleven, if you want company." Mohit didn't answer. At 11:10 the kitchen light was on, and Mohit was standing in the doorway in his socks. "Can I have the ginger one?"

qa.q: How long was the auto stuck in the underpass?
qa.a: It was stuck for forty minutes.

qa.q: What might Mohit have been feeling behind 'Whatever. It's fine'?
qa.a: Mohit was probably disappointed and hurt at not being selected, as the hidden gloves hint, but played it down to avoid drama in front of the driver; he may also simply have been tired.

qa.q: How did Shankar leave the door open without pushing?
qa.a: He held back his questions in the noisy auto and offered a clear, no-pressure time to talk, chai at eleven, whether things were fine or not.

qa.q: What was the ride like for Shankar?
qa.a: Shankar was concerned and itching to ask questions, but chose patience because the place was noisy and public.

grounding: It shows a teenager playing down disappointment with a shrug and 'fine', and a trusted adult leaving the door open instead of pressing.
